title: China's economic security offensive: How the PRC pursues dominance in industry, trade and technology
gist: Major MERICS report arguing China has moved its economic security policy onto the offensive: a 2026 wave of regulations (supply-chain security, anti-extraterritoriality, outbound investment, exit controls) builds a routinized bureaucracy to deter derisking, keep whole value chains in China and punish foreign actors. It details a Promote/Protect/Partner/Punish toolkit, warns of deindustrialization risk for Europe and middle-income economies ($1.2tn surplus, up to $650bn of G7 exports exposed), and urges bolder EU responses.

insights.claim: A mid-2026 wave of Chinese regulations is designed to counter foreign sanctions, deter foreign derisking and due diligence, and prevent outflows of technology, know-how and talent, marking a shift to offensive economic security policy.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Foreign firms in China face a materially higher regulatory and retaliation risk environment.
insights.quote: China’s leadership is going on the offensive. It combines legal and extralegal measures and uses economic coercion to defend political red lines.

insights.claim: The new rules allow broad interpretation and selective compliance with other jurisdictions, giving Beijing wiggle room from managed cooperation to escalation.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Ambiguity is a feature, so legal compliance alone won't shield companies from enforcement.

insights.claim: Recent cases involving Nuctech, Nexperia and Manus AI show how swiftly China's new foreign-facing rules can be wielded.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Precedent cases for how exposed specific companies can be caught between regimes.
insights.quote: Recent cases involving companies like Nuctech, Nexperia and Manus AI show how swiftly they can be wielded.

insights.claim: China views EU measures such as the draft Industrial Accelerator Act, revised Cybersecurity Act, Foreign Subsidies Regulation, procurement tools and forced labor ban as a compounded threat, which may accelerate coercion against Europe.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Rising probability of Chinese retaliation against European firms as EU trade defense tightens.
insights.quote: China’s coercive economic statecraft is increasingly hitting Europe, too

insights.claim: Beijing perceives multiple targeted EU regulatory measures in aggregate as 'death by a thousand cuts' that it must deter and punish, rather than as discrete issue-specific actions.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Escalation risk is nonlinear: a small new EU measure can trigger outsized retaliation.
insights.quote: what the EU may view as targeted regulatory measures are likely regarded in Beijing as a potential ‘death by a thousand cuts’

insights.claim: Since the 2014 Comprehensive National Security concept, the priority areas in China's national security doctrine have doubled from ten to twenty, many tied to economy and technology.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Securitization of more sectors expands the range of business activity that can trigger state action.

insights.claim: China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) seeks short- to medium-term resilience against trade and tech wars and long-run economic and technological dominance, including maintaining or increasing foreign dependencies on China.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Beijing deliberately aims to deepen foreign reliance on Chinese supply chains — derisking will face active resistance.
insights.quote: Maintaining and even increasing foreign dependencies on China while preventing the loss of China’s own competitive edge fit this logic.

insights.claim: Beijing's goal is to make Chinese goods and technologies indispensable across supply chains so foreigners remain dependent on China, providing growth and geopolitical leverage; it increasingly sees foreign derisking as infringing its rights.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Indispensability is a strategic objective, not a market outcome, so expect subsidies to persist regardless of returns.

insights.claim: Over the past two years Xi has repeatedly listed China's 'development interests' among its red lines in meetings with foreign leaders, and is increasingly willing to defend them with a hard hand.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Economic grievances are now treated like sovereignty issues, raising coercion risk over trade measures.

insights.claim: Official pledges to 'expand domestic demand' are less about household income than supporting upstream demand, e.g., helping consumers buy EVs mainly to support EV makers and suppliers of batteries, chips and machinery.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Don't expect a genuine consumption rebalancing; supply-side bias and export pressure continue.
insights.quote: official pledges to “expand domestic demand” (扩大内需) are less about household incomes than supporting demand upstream

insights.claim: Xi wants China to 'maintain an appropriate share of manufacturing' in GDP, and low-value manufacturers are to be upgraded rather than offshored, which hurts returns on investment but supports employment and resilience.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Persistent low-margin capacity in China means continued global price pressure and weak corporate ROI.
insights.quote: This is bad for return on investment but supports national goals by maintaining employment and building resilience.

insights.claim: MERICS classifies China's economic security tools into Promote, Protect, Partner and Punish, noting China pursues the first three on a scale and intensity far surpassing the EU's narrower approach.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Useful lens for mapping which Chinese policy levers hit which sectors.

insights.claim: Technological catch-up frees China from foreign chokeholds, while leadership in advanced technologies lets China credibly threaten to weaponize its own chokepoints.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Every Chinese tech breakthrough also increases its coercive leverage over buyers.

insights.claim: China's import-substitution playbook systematically maps supply-chain vulnerabilities, crowdsources priority lists from research bodies and industry associations, then mobilizes sectoral and local authorities with funding schemes like National Key R&D Projects and Little Giants.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Foreign suppliers of chokepoint items (chips tools, machine tools, instruments) face systematic displacement risk.
insights.quote: China’s playbook is clear: systematically map out technical supply chain vulnerabilities

insights.claim: China treats export controls not as narrow national security tools but as instruments to nurture and protect indigenous industry; the amended Foreign Trade Law (March 2026) explicitly allows controls to help establish a domestic industry.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Export controls will be used as industrial policy, making supply of critical inputs politically contingent.

insights.claim: China's export controls now extend from critical minerals to personnel such as AI engineers, and outbound investment screening was tightened from July 1, 2026 to close tech-transfer loopholes.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Chinese firms' overseas expansion and talent mobility will be more state-controlled.

insights.claim: China restricts exports of dual-use graphite and high-end lithium-ion battery technology, and closely manages rare earth magnet exports, refining equipment and even movement of rare-earth sector workers.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Non-Chinese battery and magnet supply chains face sustained input and know-how constraints.

insights.claim: Chinese SOEs like COFCO, CNPC, COSCO and China Merchants Group prioritize sending resources to China over profitability; COFCO's South American footprint now lets China hit US soybean exports.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Chinese commodity sourcing is strategic and can be redirected to punish exporters like the US.
insights.quote: These ties now empower China to hit US soybean exports.

insights.claim: China diversifies partners and avoids overreliance even on Russia, which let it largely escape the supply shock of the recent Iran war while keeping leverage over Russian fossil fuel import terms.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: China's energy security buffers reduce its vulnerability to Middle East shocks relative to peers.

insights.claim: China's punishment has escalated from 2023-24 licensing for gallium and germanium to rare-earth controls in 2025; outright bans to the US and sweeping October 9 restrictions were postponed until November 2026.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: November 2026 is a key date for critical-mineral supply risk.

insights.claim: Companies building alternative manufacturing or R&D capacity in countries like India may find plans contingent on moving assets out of China, and new rules penalize acts as vague as 'disrupting transactions with Chinese organizations'.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: China-plus-one strategies carry rising execution and legal risk.
insights.quote: stipulate penalties for actions as vague as “disrupting transactions with Chinese organizations or individuals.”

insights.claim: Beyond legal tools, China uses extralegal pressure such as indirect threats via suppliers and public boycotts, and imposed sustained economic pressure on Japan over PM Sanae Takaichi's Taiwan remarks.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Political statements can trigger commercial penalties on a country's firms.

insights.claim: The 15th FYP and 2026 State Council regulations mandate new horizontal and vertical risk monitoring, reporting and response structures across all administrative levels to map both Chinese and foreign chokepoints.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Beijing's intelligence on foreign dependencies will improve, sharpening targeted coercion.

insights.claim: Export licensing regimes require foreign companies to submit detailed supply chain information that their own home governments often lack.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Information asymmetry gives Beijing superior knowledge of Western supply-chain vulnerabilities.
insights.quote: Export licensing regimes, for instance, already require foreign companies to submit detailed supply chain information that their home governments do not always have access to.

insights.claim: Because officials' careers now revolve around spotting and addressing risks in a loyalty-driven system, routinized economic security powers likely mean more actions and a heightened risk of overreaction; foreign firms can expect more investigations and penalties.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Expect a rising base rate of Chinese probes and penalties on foreign firms in coming years.
insights.quote: Foreign governments and companies can expect more investigations, restrictions and penalties in the coming years.

insights.claim: Chinese firms and industry associations are being mobilized to share information, trigger investigations and seek financial restitution when they see their interests harmed.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Private Chinese competitors become potential triggers of state action against rivals.

insights.claim: China's punishment willingness is rising because its security definition has widened, its enforcement capacity and leverage points have grown, and internal consensus for a hard stance has strengthened.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Structural drivers imply a durable rise in coercion risk, not a cyclical one.

insights.claim: Nearly a third of China's 2025 economic growth came from exports, without which it could not meet GDP targets.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: China's growth model depends on export share gains, implying sustained pressure on trading partners.
insights.quote: In 2025, nearly a third of China’s economic growth was from exports

insights.claim: China's trade surplus grew 20% in 2025 to USD 1.2 trillion, while export value relative to volume has stagnated, reflecting industrial overcapacity.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Deflationary Chinese exports pressure global goods prices and competitors' margins.
insights.quote: Its trade surplus grew by 20 percent in 2025 to a shocking 1.2 trillion USD.

insights.claim: China hit an export record of 10 million cars in 2025, a level expected only by decade-end, and its export volumes are growing more than twice the pace of global trade.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Auto exports from China are scaling far ahead of forecasts, a key risk for incumbent automakers.

insights.claim: Rhodium Group and the US Chamber estimate up to USD 650 billion, about 12% of G7 manufacturing exports, could be directly exposed to Chinese market share gains by 2030, especially autos, machinery and chemicals.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Quantifies sector-level downside for G7 autos, machinery and chemicals exporters.
insights.quote: In aggregate, up to USD 650 billion—equivalent to around 12 percent of G7 manufacturing exports—could be directly exposed to Chinese market share gains by 2030.

insights.claim: Only about 20% of countries covered by Chinese customs run a trade surplus with China, mostly commodity exporters like Brazil, Russia, Chile, Australia and the DRC; South Korea and Taiwan are exceptions due to semiconductor trade.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Explains which economies benefit vs. lose from China's trade model and where protectionism will spread.

insights.claim: Middle-income countries such as Brazil, Turkey, Mexico and much of Southeast Asia risk having industrialization undercut by China's export surge, as China insists on holding even the low end of value chains.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Expect broadening trade defenses in emerging markets and pressure on EM manufacturing.

insights.claim: China remains far behind the frontier in lithography machines, machining tools and metrology instruments, and tightening fiscal space and squeezed profits may limit Beijing's ability to subsidize R&D at current levels.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: European/Japanese chokepoint suppliers retain leverage, but China's subsidy capacity may weaken.

insights.claim: MERICS argues the short-term pain of Chinese retaliation will be dwarfed by the medium- and long-term costs of European acquiescence.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Signals think-tank backing for tougher EU trade defense despite retaliation risk.
insights.quote: The short-term pain Beijing can inflict by waging punitive measures will arguably be dwarfed by the medium- and long-term cost of acquiescence.

insights.claim: Europe should adopt more agile trade defense, e.g., imposing provisional tariffs on all Chinese steel imports based on a preponderance of findings rather than product-by-product investigations.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Broad-based EU tariffs would be a step-change for Chinese exporters and EU producers.

insights.claim: China relies on European machine tools, metrology equipment, the lithography value chain and aerospace components, which the EU's Anti-Coercion Instrument could exploit if capitals have the political will.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Identifies European chokepoint sectors with leverage — and exposure to any escalation.

insights.claim: Derisking carries a 'first-mover disadvantage' since resilience costs efficiency, so firms won't act without mandates like stockpiling, bans on single-country sourcing and offtake agreements.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Potential policy mandates could create demand for non-Chinese suppliers of strategic inputs.
insights.quote: Any individual firm that adopts a derisking strategy will lose some level of competitiveness compared to firms that do not.

insights.claim: European companies hand massive supply chain data to Beijing for export licenses while resisting similar disclosure at home; MERICS urges national rules compelling exposure disclosure.
insights.speaker: MERICS
entities: Internal Market Emergency and Resilience Act
insights.so_what: Possible new disclosure regimes on China exposure for European firms.
insights.quote: European companies oppose similar disclosures at home, yet they have complied in China.

insights.claim: There is a current window to negotiate with China because its new laws include off-ramps and exemptions offering enforcement flexibility.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Negotiated corridors could temper worst-case escalation scenarios.
